content:
We do not yet have a lot of content about Turing machines, and also because of that, I am wondering if the current definition of Turing tape is best suited for what is to come and would like to start a discussion about it.

Background: In https://github.com/leanprover/cslib/pull/269 @Bolton Bailey added definitions for Turing machines including the current BiTape. It is similar to Mathlib's tape but uses Option Symbol instead of requiring Inhabited Symbol and ultimately is built as a structure of two Lists (the reversed left side and the right side) and a symbol (the cell at the current head).

I would like to propose a different definition and weigh the different pros and cons between them - I am not sure it is clearly better, but here it is:

structure BiTape' (Symbol : Type) where
  cells : ℤ → Option Symbol
  head : ℤ

The operations would be:

def move (t : BiTape' Symbol) : Dir → BiTape' Symbol
  | .left => { t with head := t.head - 1 }
  | .right => { t with head := t.head + 1 }

def read (t : BiTape' Symbol) :  Option Symbol  := t.cells t.head

def write (t : BiTape' Symbol) (a : Option Symbol) : BiTape' Symbol :=
  { t with cells := Function.update t.cells t.head a }

def ofList {Symbol : Type} (l : List Symbol) : BiTape' Symbol :=
  { cells := fun i => match i with
    | .ofNat n => if h : n < l.length then some l[n] else none
    | _ => none,
    head := 0 }

Now to the pros and cons:

Equality:
Two tapes in the current definition are equal if they "look" equal seen from the tape head, i.e. if you start with the empty tape and move left, you end up with the same tape. While this might be an advantage, it can also be a disadvantage, depending how you look at it. In the newly proposed definition, comparing fun i => t.cells (i - t.head) will have the same effect. In essence, in addition to how the tape looks, it also stores the head position relative to the starting position.

Execution:
I assume that actually running a Turing machine is faster using Lists than functions, i.e. pro for current definition. On the other hand, do we really need that, and wouldn't we just prove semantic equivalence to a function and evaluate that instead?

Space definition:
The space required across execution is easier with the newly proposed definition, it's just "max head position - min head position + 1". Note that the current tape definition's space requirement is buggy in a subtle way: it does not correctly factor into account when you delete symbols from the right side and add them to the left side.

Simulation in a universal Turing machine:
Having an absolute way to talk about the head position makes it easier to simulate the machine in a universal Turing machine. Updating the head position is easier than shifting the tape or recovering the head position from a shifted tape.

Finite support:
The newly proposed definition allows tapes with an infinite number of occupied cells. This is one of the hurdles in current definition: The lists have to end with a non-none cell. I don't know if we actually need this restriction on the type. It should be straightforward to prove that a tape that appears during execution must have a finite number of cells set. With the new definition, we can even easily give a bound on the positions of these set cells.

Combination of actions:
I would argue that the newly proposed definition makes it easier to argue about actions on the tapes. If you have e.g. two "move right" actions followed by a "write" action, it is almost immediate that the effect of it will be t => { head := t.head + 3, cells := Function.update t.cells (t.head + 3) s} and we have very good grind and simp support for those data structures. In the current definition, we have to deal with a sequence of List cons operations and shifting data between .right, .head and .left, two of which are again a custom type (StackTape) which needs its own simp and grind lemmas.

I might have missed several aspects and I'm happy to hear your opinion!

Tagging some people who I assume would be interested: @Samuel Schlesinger @Maximilian Keßler @Sorrachai Yingchareonthawornchai
I find it a bit counterintuitive that the head is part of the 'tape'. Shouldn't it be part of the 'machine', i.e., be somewhere else?

After all, if the tape were infinite only in one direction, we'd just use ωSequence to represent such tape, wouldn't we?

So I guess what I'm saying is to consider whether it'd make sense to make a generalisation of ωSequence (ωBiSequence?) and then choose a more descriptive name for your structure as well as generalise the type of Symbol, e.g.,

structure Memory (Symbol : Type*) where
  cells : ωBiSequence
  head : ℤ

(Edit, forgot to say:) I agree that bundling the head in there might be advantageous, so I'm looking forward to seeing more comments about this.

Fabrizio Montesi said:

I find it a bit counterintuitive that the head is part of the 'tape'. Shouldn't it be part of the 'machine', i.e., be somewhere else?

Sorry for the spam, apparently some papers do indeed call that a tape with its 'head' and 'cells', and some don't.. darn. :-)

I guess the main question is if we want to move the head (newly proposed) or the tape (current definition) and if we want to use functions or lists. What to bundle is a different matter. And of course if it is important to disallow infinitely occupied tapes.
Not sure about omegasequence. What is the advantage over Nat -> Symbol?

ah sorry, ωSequence is essentially Nat -> Symbol. I think I would prefer to stay with Int -> Option Symbol instead of adding an abstraction on top, essentially because the tape already provides an abstraction, but we can see.

chris477 said:

Not sure about omegasequence. What is the advantage over Nat -> Symbol?

It is a just one field structure for ℕ → α that we define in CSLib. Just an attempt to have some common operations on sequences. (And there were various objections to docs#Stream')

Fabrizio Montesi said:

Fabrizio Montesi said:

I find it a bit counterintuitive that the head is part of the 'tape'. Shouldn't it be part of the 'machine', i.e., be somewhere else?

Sorry for the spam, apparently some papers do indeed call that a tape with its 'head' and 'cells', and some don't.. darn. :-)

Then again, there can be multi-head machines. But let's not get stuck on naming at this stage.
Space complexity needs to separate working space and input space. That’s how you get logspace classes

Fabrizio Montesi said:

Then again, there can be multi-head machines. But let's not get stuck on naming at this stage.

Yeah I think multiple heads per tape is a rather obscure topic where we probably don’t need to get into (as opposed to multiple tapes with one head per tape of course, as shreyas mentioned), although the newly proposed version would be closer to supporting those.
Do we have any textbooks for reference for the formalization? Or do we formalize ourselves from scratch?

Chris Henson said:

And there were various objections to docs#Stream'

What were the objections?

Sorrachai Yingchareonthawornchai schrieb:

Do we have any textbooks for reference for the formalization? Or do we formalize ourselves from scratch?

I've been using Wagner-Wechsung, which is quite old but super detailed. For the question of this thread, textbooks won't be of much help - it's mostly about ergonomics of proofs in lean, and furthermore, textbooks are usually based on set theory and thus won't use List. Configurations are usually encoded as functions Int -> Symbol plus an integer for the head position or functions Int -> (Symbol x Bool) or something similar. But of course, a textbook is very helpful in finding e.g. the correct way to define an input / read-only tape (e.g. can the head move beyond the input or not - in the book I have been using this is a "no"). There are other "fragile" definitions like oracles for space-bounded machines.

Eric Wieser said:

Chris Henson said:

And there were various objections to docs#Stream'

What were the objections?

I argued for Stream' and didn't follow all the arguments, but part of the discussion was about the difference between streams and sequences. I.e. that while Stream' is defined as ℕ → α, this is meant to be an implementation detail because we can't define coinductive data.

See discussion following #mathlib4 > Why is Stream' called Stream'? @ 💬 for instance.

I played around a bit with the definition and I think that tracking the position explicitly is a bit annoying because of the redundancy with the tape being shifted. The main advantage would be that the space definition is "obviously" correct. Without it, we need to define a function that represents the head's position relative to the starting position across execution steps and then we need to justify that "max pos - min pos + 1" captures what we mean by space. One justification could be that if the tape is initially empty and the TM uses space s according to that definition, then at most s cells of the tape are non-empty. But still, I think the function-based definition is easier to work with than the List-based definition.

@chris477 your definition captures space complexity more accurately than before, but it still has a drawback. I can just pile up space complexity by skipping a lot of tape cells and writing after them. This is consequential in lower bound proofs. I ran into this issue in some private Algolean code. Fwiw I agree that integer indices are better to have for two distinct reasons.

I think we can do better by defining space and time complexity on configuration traces of TMs as follows:

  1. Thanks to your indices we can trivially deduce the set of input cells. Let’s call it III

  2. We iterate over the configuration trace of a TM and track the set of cells we write to (let’s say WWW). We also track the length of the tm configuration trace.

  3. We define space complexity as the cardinality of the W∖IW \setminus IW∖I

Basically a configuration trace is a recursive structure that looks exactly like circuits. I sketched out a design suggestion below :

A Sketch for Configuration Traces of a TM.

There is a leaf config which is any valid initial configuration. There are actions you can take on the Turing machine such as “read head”, “write to head cell”, “move head left/right/not at all”. Each of these moves corresponds to a constructor that takes an input config (and a tape number). A semantic function computes the TMs trace. This can be used to disallow writes on read only input tapes.

I'm not really sure what you mean by "skipping". To make sure we are talking about the same thing: In the literature I know, just moving across a tape cell without writing (or without modifying its contents) counts as "space used". To sidestep the issue about how exactly the input factors into space requirements, there usually is a separate input tape where the head is not allowed to write and also not allowed to move (far) beyond the initially written contents. In this case, the space requirement of the input tape is counted as zero.
What I was worried about in my previous message is that the "step" semantics and the "headPosition" definition are a decoupled. We should have some kind of way to make sure that the cell where the TM writes is the same as the one designated by "headPosition". This is trivial if the head position is part of the structure that describes the tape, but it is more involved if the tape is shifted and there is no explicit head position as part of the configuration.

“Skipping” => assume your TM is initialised. The first n cells of your read tape are language symbols. The rest are ⊥\bot⊥. By skipping, I mean letting a large number of tape cells after input be ⊥\bot⊥ and writing after them. These cells are unused and wouldn’t count towards space complexity by any meaningful definition. Textbooks paper over this because they assume that we always write to the TM in contiguous chunks. So they can do as you suggest I.e. count any skipped cells in the space consumed. If they indeed want this extra space to be counted, they pad the input, by writing some standard default character on to those extra cells. We can’t paper over this in the formal version. There is a distinction between TMs with and without padded inputs.

The most explicit definition of (auxiliary) space complexity is “number of non-input cells this TM wrote to as a function on input size”. The total space complexity is simply “input size + auxiliary space complexity”

I think I disagree here. The textbook I am following defines space as "the number of worktape squares visited by one of the heads". The same textbook requires the head on a read-only input tape (which then does not count towards space used) to not move beyond the pre-written content for more than one square/cell. I think the reason for that is that if you let a tape head move beyond the written content at no space cost, you can use it as a counter free of charge.

I don't understand that argument. Firstly by moving beyond the input, you still incur time complexity costs. Secondly you would need a way to keep track of how far you move for the counter to make sense. Given a fixed state size, you can at most move a constant number of steps to keep track of how far you move forward and back. Thus you can traverse at most Θ(1)\Theta(1)Θ(1) cells to use as a counter and you would still need to mark the cell at which you stop and return to the input cells. Secondly this restriction is only applied to the input tape, so if simulating counters were an issue before, they can still be an issue in the work tapes.

Thirdly there are situations where you might want to actually traverse a fixed number of ⊥\bot⊥ cells to write something in reverse order. Trivial example off the top of my head : iterate over a list of fixed-bit-width integer inputs and output their bit-reversed version.

Further your textbook only applies this rule to the read tape of a multi-tape machine. Thus its definition of space complexity does not extend to single tape machines where we necessarily have to move past the input. My definition covers both single and multi tape situations. Given all this, I am fairly convinced your textbook is making an assumption that is convenient for its authors but not for formalisation.

So you are trying to discount the pre-filled input on single-tape machines? Without a textbook, I don't feel confident in finding a good definition for that. But indeed, with a single tape and a single head, it doesn't make a difference if we allow the input head to move beyond the input because of the finite control.

Just to have this documented here, for the case of multi-tape (or multi-head on a single tape) Turing machines, if we do not include empty cells the head moves across (and have a special discounted input tape) into the space requirement we can decide {0ⁿ 1 0ⁿ | n ∈ ℕ} in constant space. Thus, in this model, we could accept non-regular languages in constant space, which is usually not what you want.

This is how it works: Start by checking that the input conforms to 010. Then move the input head to the left end of the input. Put a marker on the work tape. Then move the input and the work head to the right synchronously. After we reach the 1, continue moving the work head to the left while moving the input head to the right. +- some constants, accept if and only if the input head reaches the end of the input at the same time the work head reaches the marker.

I am not suggesting excluding the input cells entirely. I am suggesting a two-fold definition:

  1. Auxiliary space complexity. Space used outside input cells.
  2. Total space complexity. The above + input size.

Concretely I might to be able to state the definitions of L and NL, and let's say prove Savitch's theorem.
With your definition, what I am thinking of is space complexity of machines with and without input padding being identical, which makes no sense to me (think space-hierarchy theorem).

As for additional references, the Barak-Arora book definition is fairly standard. I don't think any standard textbook definition will necessarily cover all edge cases that are formalisation-relevant though.

Arora-Barak does indeed define space as the number of cells that are non-empty at some point of execution. I find that weird and also I would challenge that it is easier to formalize than the cells moved across. They also require start markers, which I would also try to avoid due to the complications wrt the alphabet. So in general, I'm not sure we should follow that book, at least for the foundations since the proofs are not super detailed. In the pdf you linked, there is an exercise that states that this definition has the property that SPACE(log log n) = SPACE(0) (which is consistent with my remark about regular languages above). The complexity zoo states that while there are different definitions of log log space, it is a class that is extensively studied. So I don't think we should exclude this class.

Concerning padding: I don't follow your argument. Since the purpose of padding is to modify the input length instead of the behaviour or absolute (as opposed to relative to the input length) space requirement, padding does influence space complexity also in the "cells moved across"-definition.
Note that even to define LOGLOG, you need an auxiliary space complexity definition. Your current definition includes inputs by default.

I would exclude the input if some syntactic conditions are met, as is custom. Otherwise you cannot even properly define log. We would also need a special output tape of course. But I think we have strayed quite far from the topic of this thread.
Yes. Maybe a separate topic on space complexity is merited starting here #CSLib > Turing tape definition @ 💬

About padding, it is still customary to maintain the original input size where it is used, and describe space complexity in terms of this original size. What I mean concretely w.r.t padding is, one can move without writing the padded input for the equivalent number of cells. Under your definition, these cells still count in space complexity.
No they don’t, since they are inputs. Do you have an opinion on List vs function and if tapes should in principle allow an infinite number of occupied cells?

I favour functions because it enables the design I described above and because it lets us trivially reason about the tapes and the index of their contents independent of the head position and whether or not new symbols are appended on either end. The current bitape structure, which is a list zipper in functional data structure terminology , presents different structures for the same tape depending on where the head is.

I agree that the head should be bundled with the tape, in my experience that is useful to have when dealing with turing machines. Also it means we can have better dot-notation for accessing the symbol at the head. Hearing your discussion, this seems to be rather consensus.

Regarding the question of whether to use ω(Bi)Sequence, I don't really see why we would ever need that in a Turing machine. Maybe I'm just misinformed, but unless we have a clear usecase where we want that there can be infinitely many (non-none values) on the tape, I would be against introducing it. One nice property is in fact that if we want to take the output of a tape, we have the guarantee that we can yield a finite list (typically, everything to the right of the head until the first none encountered). I would like there to exist a function output : Configuration of a TM → List Γ (I'll address this question in a different thread as well, currently, this is not the case for the SingleTapeTM in CSLib).

As a result of that, I don't like a potential transition to ω(Bi)Sequence, and similarly the BiTape' outlined in @chris477's initial post here, because it would also allow non-finite tapes.

And if we want to have the finite-support guarantee as part of the definition of a Turing Machine (which I would suggest we keep), then to me using a tape like it is implemented right now seems like the correct thing to do, because it is the most natural way to me to represent it. In particular, using a function + proof of finite support makes things noncomputable as soon as we try to ask questions like "Give me a list representation of the tape" (unless we also track a specific bound, which is not the job of such a data structure but rather proof-related).

However, I do agree that it is nice to view a tape as ℤ → Option Symbol sometimes. In my previous Turing machine work, I ended up using this at times, and thus (essentially) formalized the natural equivalence that tapes can be represented by finite-support functions ℤ → Option Symbol, and then lemmas relating these two / constructing from one another. I found it good to work with the List version internally in the definition, and then in proof contexts transition to ℤ → Option Symbol whenever needed using some lemmas.

Also, I think that the current implementation (with equivalence classes of lists) is (probably / in my opinion) closest to common textbook sources that I am aware of, in the sense that it naturally models what people usually think of when the word Turing machine comes up.

Thus, my suggestion would be to keep the Tape definition as is, and add appropriate definitions / theorems to prove equivalence to finite-support functions ℤ → Option Symbol.

I'd be interested in your opinions on this @chris477 @Fabrizio Montesi @Sorrachai Yingchareonthawornchai
Why is controversial to have infinite tapes? TMs by definition have unbounded tapes.

The suggested translation to int indexed version from Bitape will be too complicated. You can easily index relative to the current tape head, but what is useful is an absolute and fixed index independent of heads. The bitape version makes it impossible to have a definition of tape indices that is independent of the head of the TM, as more cells are added or cells are removed.

I think @chris477 has the right design. Our disagreement on space complexity is minor and I can remedy it in Algolean to make it work for complexity theorists (the Barak Arora definition essentially)
Yes, they have unbounded tapes by definition, but also they usually require that the tape has finite support.

You can never reach a tape with infinite support in a finite number of steps anyway. So this is guaranteed by either definition for terminating procedures.

Arguably you should allow infinite support in the case of semi definite procedures. The bitape defintion doesn’t allow this. This is trivial for the int-indexed version
There have been several discussions about adding a generalization of Finsupp to mathlib. See #Is there code for X? > Finsupp-like partial function

The point about being able to extract the output from the tape is a good one, although I’m not sure it is really a problem: yes, you need an existential quantifier but usually you prove equivalence to a computable function anyway most of the time, so the noncomputability of extracting the output should not be too big of an issue. I can live with staying with the current definition, we can always go via https://github.com/leanprover/cslib/pull/499 if needed, I just thought we could maybe spare us some of the complexity coming from having to define two more structures like BiTape and StackTape if all we need is already captured in Int -> Option Symbol.
Thinking about it a bit more, I do see the problem with extracting the output.

Although, in a very crude way, one could “look” left and right of the head for t cells to find everything that could have been written ok yeah plus the size of the input for a single tape machine and providing all that via the configuration sequence. But yeah, probably not worth it :sweat_smile:
Looking forward to your pull request(s)!
